item.description: Hedge funds across nearly all mainstream strategies lost money simultaneously in October, showing that most gains over the past year were actually from implicit long AI exposure, not genuine diversified strategy returns.
item.content:encoded:
Hedge funds across nearly all mainstream strategies lost money simultaneously in October, showing that most gains over the past year were actually from implicit long AI exposure, not genuine diversified strategy returns.

To understand how last month's "perfect storm" happened and which funds truly decoupled (like Citadel), this episode provides specific position and risk control figures.

4:10 Flagship funds claiming stability lost money collectively in October
Millennium, Point72, and Exodus Point—the funds with the most concentrated talent and assets, viewed by investors as most steadfast during crises—all lost money in October. Millennium, with ~14% annualized returns, fell 2.3% in a single month. By hedge fund logic, this is dereliction: investors buy hedge funds not to beat bull markets but to expect protection during downturns. In October, that protection failed entirely. The real shock is not the loss itself but the failure to hedge.

8:20 Funds claiming diversification were concentrated in the same few AI stocks
Vara, a fund with positions highly overlapping with certain AI narratives, crashed 33% in October yet remains positive year-to-date—showing how much that prior AI exposure returned. Whale Rock similarly fell 12%. These single-strategy funds' exposure is explicit: nearly all positions bet on the same small handful of AI stocks. When momentum reverses, no hedge can cushion the blow.

12:33 Data shows multi-strategy funds were herding into the same stocks
Pivotal Path's research shows the top 10 multi-strategy funds control ~$2.2 trillion in positions including leverage, yet the actual capital supporting those positions is only $300-350 billion—indicating extreme system leverage. This does not mean they were momentum trading; likely these firms independently judged but converged on the same liquid stocks that fit their risk frameworks. The danger lies in what happens when they all change their minds at once: forced selling cascades in sync, exactly as occurred in October.

15:40 Multi-strategy funds show no mercy to losing traders
Nishant explained the brutal internal risk controls of multi-strategy funds: a PM managing $100 loses 5% (=$5) and their allocation gets cut in half; if they continue to 7.5% total loss, they are force-liquidated and fired on the spot. This discipline is the core pitch of the multi-strategy model—prevent any one team's losses from dragging down the whole platform. But when all strategies turned bad at once in October, this very mechanism meant massive positions were cut simultaneously, actually accelerating the decline.

24:51 Money rushed to buy shares but top platforms closed to new capital
Millennium aimed to raise $20 billion this year, received over $30 billion in demand, ultimately took $22 billion. Meanwhile, D.E. Shaw, Point72, and Citadel combined returned $35-40 billion to investors. A paradox emerges: investors desperately want multi-strategy fund slots, yet the top platforms are capping size and returning capital. The reason: once you add enough teams, new positions no longer add real diversification—they just dilute the same underlying risk.

29:59 Thursday's crash was not emotion but mechanical chain reaction
Michael Ball attributes Thursday's crash to options market mechanics: when investors buy puts for downside protection, put sellers (market makers) must continuously sell to hedge their delta risk as prices fall, which itself depresses prices in a self-reinforcing spiral. Layer on leveraged ETFs, systematic vol-control strategies, and CTA trend-following funds all forced to cut positions on the same day—four mechanisms in sync—and you breach the S&P level that held for months.

37:05 New cloud operators halved in value, rate sensitivity is the weakness
Take Iron: a cloud stock once pitched as "Bitcoin miners transitioning to AI compute." Its price was $77 in November 2025, down to $21 at recording—roughly a 70% fall. These companies borrowed heavily to build data centers and are highly sensitive to interest rates and customer prepayment quality. Ball thinks the selloff is excessive because backlog orders and compute demand remain robust. But whether 2028 new projects get regulatory blocked remains genuinely unresolved.

41:11 Huang's governance turmoil failed to ripple through the market
Markets might have feared that Nvidia governance trouble would transmit through the AI chain. But Ball observed the actual impact was limited: Nvidia itself declined modestly and AI/semiconductor stocks rebounded days later. His reading: AI is now too large for Nvidia or Anthropic alone to move the needle. One company's governance headline cannot shake the whole narrative anymore. Stock moves now track mechanical forces like short covering more than fundamental narrative shifts.

item.title: Architects don't compete with others, only with a hundred versions of themselves
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-11-11-tanpai-建筑师不与别人竞争-只跟一百个自己赛跑/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-11-11-tanpai-建筑师不与别人竞争-只跟一百个自己赛跑/
item.description: She says she never felt like she was racing the rat race because she had no one to race against in the first place—architect Qi Shanshan's (戚山山) vitality doesn't come from self-discipline, but from asking herself first whether she actually likes something before deciding to do it.
item.content:encoded:
She says she never felt like she was racing the rat race because she had no one to race against in the first place—architect Qi Shanshan's (戚山山) vitality doesn't come from self-discipline, but from asking herself first whether she actually likes something before deciding to do it.

This episode's information density is moderate—it's more a complete showcase of one person's lifestyle. But two points of conversation are worth pausing to reflect on your own decision-making: the logic of wanting-it-all versus choosing what you truly want, and the concept of playing it safe.

4:06 Female team members, measuring with their bodies, built truer than blueprints
The construction site of the Tengchong An zhi Ruo Su project was staffed almost entirely by women from the village. They threw bricks up along more than thirty meters and over one hundred steps, relaying materials up the stairs. Qi Shanshan discovered the villagers couldn't read blueprints, so she told them: ‘Listen to your body—turn when your body tells you to.’ They laid bricks by feel. When finished and checked against the blueprints, it was nearly identical. The sections built precisely according to specification, by contrast, looked stiff and lacked spirit.

7:06 Brilliance comes from deviation and error, never from mere precision
She says she's always fought against the rigid rule of ‘must be perfectly horizontal and vertical.’ Why must stairs go straight up, then make a 180-degree turn? No one walks that way—mountain paths are walked on a slant. She believes all the beautiful moments come from error, deviation, misalignment—from the non-dogmatic places, not from precision itself. Refined technique is the foundation, but what truly moves people comes from respecting nature's irregularity, not from rules imposed by people.

10:06 Fear you direct at yourself is more powerful than external punishment
Her father disciplined her harshly: he'd strike her fingers when she played a wrong note, beat her even for a score of 99 out of 100, saying it was an attitude problem. After she moved to the US at 14, she finally escaped direct supervision. But she wrote her father's name on a piece of paper and taped it on her desk. Whenever she thought of getting up to play, she'd see the name and scare herself back into studying. She'd transformed his external strictness into a self-monitoring mechanism she maintained herself, not into simple consequence-free abandon.

17:11 How you carry yourself determines what energy the world sends back
Her mother was a dancer. Caring for several elderly relatives and her injured father at once, physically depleted to the point of collapse, ‘she stood right up, took a lipstick from her pocket, applied it, and went back to work’—because ‘no one was watching.’ Her logic: if you go to work without makeup and looking miserable, people see you as pitiful, and the feedback they send you is negative energy. With lipstick on, they see vitality, and the feedback that comes back is positive energy. ‘So in our family it became the norm: don't complain, don't spiral—and happiness just naturally follows.’

20:13 Working all night for satisfaction is different from racing against others
Harvard's architecture program kept her working from 9 AM to 5 AM. When tired, she'd run for half an hour and come back to keep working. She completed her degree before the phrase ‘racing the rat race’ became common, and she never felt like she was doing it. Knocking off at 5 AM, even exhausted, she was happy—she'd stopped actively because she was satisfied, not because she was forced to. She says those years didn't train her in design skills, but in ‘how to find satisfaction.’

27:40 One hundred meters of dining hall became the seed of rural transformation
In a poor village deep in the Qinling Mountains near Hanzhong, girls couldn't attend school because their families couldn't afford lunch fees. The school found a solution: join the soccer team, get free lunch. With no construction land available, the team converted a narrow hundred-meter-long old stable into a cafeteria, using food-service practices from train cars to have children line up in two queues. The team later made it to the provincial squad. The training camp brought parents for coaching, creating needs for housing and hotels, which drove expansion of the fields, reconstruction of the primary school, and a visitor center. Over six or seven years, one cafeteria rolled into complete rural revival, driven by a group of young girls who had no idea they'd changed their village.

1:05:32 Rest you've approved but don't actually want isn't rest, it's procrastination
The host reflected on her habit of thinking ‘I have this already—how do I add that to it?’ Qi Shanshan pointed out: this is playing it safe. You've approved downtime and fitness as ‘wonderful things’ in your head, but they're not things you actually want to do, which is why they're at the bottom of your to-do list, not the first thing you want to do when you wake up. Her logic isn't wanting-it-all—it's: ‘What do I actually love doing most?’ Then put that first in your day.

1:11:34 AI makes renderings beautiful; humans do the work clients actually need
She doesn't oppose using AI—when she and her colleagues learned architecture twenty years ago, the parametric design they used was already a programming tool. What she opposes is blind hope—outsourcing all the analysis and thinking you should be doing yourself to AI, then not using the time saved to do something more valuable. She says the truly irreplaceable work is face-to-face communication with clients: where is their confusion, what do they want to become? That's deep work requiring you to feel the relationship between people and space on site. AI in the studio handles only surface-level work: making renderings beautiful.

item.title: Plato said authentic philosophical teaching cannot be written down
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-11-10-verybad-柏拉图说真正的哲学教诲根本不能被写下来/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-11-10-verybad-柏拉图说真正的哲学教诲根本不能被写下来/
item.description: In the Seventh Letter, Plato says he never wrote down his true philosophical teaching because philosophy is not purely propositional but a kind of experience; the dialogue form exists precisely to carry what cannot be written.
item.content:encoded:
In the Seventh Letter, Plato says he never wrote down his true philosophical teaching because philosophy is not purely propositional but a kind of experience; the dialogue form exists precisely to carry what cannot be written.

The second half's discussion of why Plato wrote dialogues is information-dense with layered arguments; the first 20-plus minutes on Texas elections and a golf politicization paper play more like warm-up chat and can be skipped.

7:10 Political disagreement really can ruin your putt
A paper by Berkeley and Yale researchers claims professional golfers perform worse in politically mixed groups, with the effect strengthening as partisan intensity increases. The hosts question the methodology: players' political views are mostly inferred from Twitter posts and donation records, which itself introduces selection bias—actual conservatives who dislike publicity might never be identified at all. Moreover, the paper never measured any anxiety or interaction, yet directly concludes this is ‘political heterogeneity causing psychological tension’. Both hosts think the effect itself may be real but find insufficient evidence for attributing it to political disagreement.

34:26 Plato says authentic philosophy cannot be written
According to the Seventh Letter, which is widely believed to be authentically from Plato, Plato says he never wrote down his true philosophical teaching because it simply cannot be written. The reason: every written work presupposes that a philosophical position can be exhaustively laid out as a series of propositions. But for Plato, philosophy is not purely propositional—at least part of it is an experience related to what the Phaedrus calls ‘divine madness’. So Plato needs a form that can present arguments and also present this non-propositional experience—and that is why the dialogue form exists.

48:33 No conclusion is deliberate: Plato's design
The hosts point out that many of Plato's dialogues deliberately offer no conclusion—so-called aporetic dialogues—like the Euthyphro, which disputes throughout about ‘what is piety’ yet reaches no answer. This is not failure but design: once you give a conclusion, the reader stops thinking, just as Socrates criticizes writing for ‘making people stop remembering’. Tamler quotes David Lynch for comparison—‘closure’ is just an excuse to make you forget what you just saw; anything truly alive should leave you still thinking, still arguing after you finish.

50:35 Two conceptions of truth: proposition versus process
Dave proposes a new idea: Plato actually operates with two different conceptions of truth. One is propositional—like mathematics, you present your argument, others either believe it or they don't, and that's the end of it. The other is processual—truth is not something you can fit into a sentence and hand to someone else, but something you can only approach through sustained questioning and participation. If you hold the latter conception, what you can do is not ‘give an answer’ but get the other person to ‘keep thinking this way’. The hosts believe this is the deep reason Plato refused to write philosophy as a checklist of propositions.

57:42 Dialogue is shadow, yet shadow can lead from the cave
Plato says in the Republic that art is a threefold imitation of reality (Form—concrete thing—artistic depiction), often read as a devaluation of art. But Highland argues this framework actually explains the value of the dialogue: the dialogue itself is an imitation or image of ‘philosophical dialogue’ as such. Plato even often has dialogues reported second or third hand, deliberately emphasizing this is a ‘shadow’ that passes through layers. Yet a good imitation can lead the viewer toward the very reality it imitates—dialogue as philosophy's image can lead readers toward actually doing philosophy.

1:02:47 Philosophy conferences reserve half time for questions; papers do not
The hosts compare academic conferences in philosophy and psychology. Psychology conferences typically run 45 minutes of talks and 15 minutes of questions, often leaving things unresolved. Philosophy conferences follow the convention of splitting time equally between presentation and questions, sometimes giving questions more time, because everyone agrees ‘philosophy really happens in the question-and-answer session’. Yet ironically, philosophers accept this in conference format but when writing journal papers fail to bring any of this dialogical character into the text itself—response articles appear years after publication, already a different kind of philosophical inquiry.

1:06:49 Is Socrates in the Crito playing a part?
Highland argues that Socrates in the Apology is radical and uncompromising, yet three weeks later in the Crito he meekly says ‘Athens is my parent, I must honor my covenant with the law’—completely different people. He infers Socrates' arguments were actually aimed at Crito, to keep Crito's soul from falling, not reasons Socrates himself genuinely believed. Tamler disagrees with this split judgment—he thinks Socrates could well genuinely believe this ‘covenant with law’ argument. The quiet tone after accepting the sentence is simply not contradictory to the passionate tone of defending himself; there's no need to strain and explain it as ‘this is what he's saying to someone else’.

1:13:56 Socrates' death is the highest form of comedy
At the paper's end, Highland argues that Socrates' composure facing death represents the highest form of comedy: comedy won at the price of acknowledging tragedy, yet transcending tragic lamentation. Socrates grasps the tragic situation of philosophy but does not react like a tragic hero; instead he faces it with a smile from the ‘divine’ perspective. The hosts recall the end of the Symposium, where Socrates tries to convince the comic playwright Aristophanes and the tragic playwright Agathon that ‘one person should be able to write both tragedy and comedy’—in Plato's hands, Socrates himself is often a comic figure, like Bugs Bunny, poking fun at others for enjoyment.

item.title: Competitor 100x larger, yet overtaken in downloads: scale is not a moat
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-11-10-latentspace-体量大100倍的对手-却被下载量反超-规模不是护城河/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-11-10-latentspace-体量大100倍的对手-却被下载量反超-规模不是护城河/
item.description: A founder with no email background overtook downloads through product experience, while Twilio—inventor of DevRel—acquired SendGrid but left it dormant.
item.content:encoded:
A founder with no email background overtook downloads through product experience, while Twilio—inventor of DevRel—acquired SendGrid but left it dormant.

The founder discusses concrete engineering details: IP pools, MCP permission models, changes to AI search pages—relevant for anyone building developer-first products or managing growth influenced by AI recommendations.

0:00 Once thought beating SendGrid impossible, now doubling his lead
Zeno Rocha recalls early fears SendGrid was ‘impossible’ to beat. This year, Resend's npm downloads surpassed SendGrid—now more than double. Resend serves 4.3M users, just crossed 120k+ paying customers including Warner Brothers and HBO, plus a Japanese group that purchased ~20k domains in one transaction.

15:48 Trust users first, police behavior after, not before
Most email providers require signup forms and 2-day manual review, rejecting most applications. Zeno rejects this model: instead of imprisoning users for eighteen years before proving they deserve freedom, he flips it. Default trust, then immediately block on hard signals like bounce rates and complaints—since most issues stem from misuse, not abuse.

30:31 A hundred times larger, yet unable to win with scale
Twilio was 100x Resend's size at the start, yet couldn't crush it through scale. The conversation landed on a judgment: commodity businesses like email have no scale advantage. Product quality is all that matters. Twilio, which invented DevRel, now appears to coast on past laurels, underinvesting in SendGrid and SMS.

34:50 From leasing AWS SES to owning the entire sending stack
Resend started on AWS SES, differentiating on developer UX. Now building in-house: acquiring and managing IP pools, establishing carrier relationships, switching email delivery from Node.js to Go for speed. The goal is finer observability—previously the platform couldn't see whether a sent email reached the inbox, spam folder, or promotions tab.

40:26 One MCP forced a complete rebuild of permission systems
Resend's first MCP was a local version written part-time by Yoko, an a16z investor. Growth demanded a remote MCP, but that required OAuth and RBAC first. They redesigned the entire account permissions system from scratch, only then moving to distribution and the official plugin marketplace.

43:47 Eighty tools didn't confuse the model; data density did
The industry feared many MCP tools would confuse models; Cloudflare even capped theirs at two. Resend went opposite: ~20 at launch, now 80+. Tool quantity itself hasn't caused confusion. The real issue is single calls returning too much data, losing information. Achieving feature parity with the dashboard—billing, team invites, account deletion—is extremely hard.

1:01:17 AI miscalculated pricing, so he copied the price list to markdown
Zeno asked AI to compare Resend against competitors' cost for 1.2M emails—the numbers came back wrong, and the model claimed Resend ‘pricing is opaque’. The problem: AI won't execute JavaScript calculator widgets on the page. Fix: duplicate the numbers as plain text in a markdown version of the same page. Fixed in days, but now maintaining two content sources with no single source of truth.

1:21:06 Better a smaller company his daughter actually wants to spend time with
A YC partner told Zeno his design perfectionism was slowing progress—it stung, but was fair. He clarified his priorities: in ten years, he'd rather have $10M revenue and a daughter who wants to play with him than $100M and a distant relationship. He carried this priority back into parenting decisions.

item.title: Individual neuron meanings are far less confused than imagined; agents find answers through systematic interrogation
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-11-10-cogrev-单个神经元的含义没有想象中混乱-智能体逐个审问找到答案/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-11-10-cogrev-单个神经元的含义没有想象中混乱-智能体逐个审问找到答案/
item.description: Gated MLPs force neurons to switch between a handful of meanings, not hundreds mixed together. AI agents running systematic experiments can write descriptions that accurately predict neuron behavior, overturning the old claim that neurons are too chaotic to interpret.
item.content:encoded:
Gated MLPs force neurons to switch between a handful of meanings, not hundreds mixed together. AI agents running systematic experiments can write descriptions that accurately predict neuron behavior, overturning the old claim that neurons are too chaotic to interpret.

If you care about why large models hallucinate and how to monitor them, this episode offers a new path: reading neurons directly without auxiliary models, backed by quantifiable, reproducible metrics.

7:18 Single neurons are far more interpretable than academia assumed
Tigges's core claim: individual neurons in MLPs have been underestimated by prior interpretability work. Early networks were smaller and messier, and activation functions like ReLU and GELU were hard to parse, so the field defaulted to ‘representations are distributed, not in single neurons’ and relied on auxiliary models like SAEs instead. His counter: you rarely need many neurons firing at once; even if one neuron encodes multiple meanings, it's usually ‘a compact cluster of meanings,’ not hundreds of inseparable semantic stacks.

18:04 Gated structures let one neuron hold two different meanings
Modern models use SwiGLU gated MLPs that give each neuron two independent signals: the result of gate projection multiplied by up projection, forming AND-gate-like logic. This lets the same neuron switch interpretations across contexts—Tigges's example is a neuron where one pole represents ‘oral health’ and the other ‘marine wildlife,’ with completely different downstream neurons pre-positioned by context to receive the right signal and avoid misreading.

27:14 Ablating 88% of activations barely dents model performance
On Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, the team kept only the top-64 strongest activations per active expert (512 neurons total, keeping 64), suppressing roughly 88% of activations and zeroing the rest; another approach kept only extreme values per neuron across historical percentiles, replacing the rest with near-zero means. Result: model performance on many benchmarks stayed roughly flat compared to the original; the only clear degradation was in reasoning—loops, repeated self-checking—but simple subsequent fine-tuning restored performance to or beyond original levels.

37:32 Without internal noise, models become more confident
Why do some reasoning-free benchmarks actually score higher after cutting most neurons? Tigges explains these benchmarks measure how fast the model answers, and with less internal noise to distract, the most confident answer floats to the top without interference. For reasoning tasks, the same effect appears after fine-tuning—the model finds the answer it already knows faster, without repeated self-doubt.

51:09 74% KL divergence recovery validates neuron function descriptions
The way to verify whether a neuron function description is sound: completely ablate the neuron, have another model score each token's predicted activation 0-9 based only on the description, feed those predictions back in, and measure how much it recovers the damaged next-token prediction distribution (KL divergence). The main metric is 74% KL divergence recovery weighted by damage magnitude—not 74% accuracy, not ‘the model is 74% understood,’ but at positions where the neuron actually matters, predictions roughly match the real activations.

56:07 The monosemanticity question is the wrong question
Tigges says ‘is this neuron monosemantic or multisemantic’ itself is misleading; the real question is whether you can enumerate everything it represents. His hypothetical: a neuron that might respond to clothing, exercise equipment, dishes, and tablecloths—looks multivalent, but if the model's underlying concept is ‘things you'd see at a garage sale,’ humans might never discover that connection. Many neurons are better understood as verbs than nouns: not detecting an entity, but signaling downstream to trigger wait states, rechecks, direction changes in reasoning control flow.

1:21:31 Facts live in connections, not neurons
Tigges flags a counterintuitive problem: models have around 5 million neurons, but clearly remember far more facts because one neuron ≠ one fact; facts live in connections between neurons—the number of paths a few dozen interconnected neurons can combine is exponential. His example: a small ‘community’ of dozens of neurons dedicated to encoding which painters belong to Impressionism, Neo-Impressionism, or Post-Impressionism. Verified experts also show strong topic consistency, mostly covering one to three subjects.

1:37:01 100 million tokens of fine-tuning brings reasoning back
After sparsity, reasoning degrades—loops, self-checking, indecision—but Tigges says that's not lost knowledge, it's miscalibration. The team used roughly 100 million tokens, a few GPUs, and one day of subsequent fine-tuning to restore or partly exceed original performance, verified on math, code, and medical QA benchmarks. He emphasizes this is far below standard post-training scale and vastly below pre-training scale, showing the ablated 90% of activations affected whether the model could smoothly find an answer, not whether it knew one.

item.title: China's AI didn't overtake through homegrown innovation—it runs on rented American compute and copied American models
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-11-10-eightythousand-中国ai没有自研超车-靠的是租美国算力-抄美国模型/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-11-10-eightythousand-中国ai没有自研超车-靠的是租美国算力-抄美国模型/
item.description: Chinese models lag American ones by about six months, but this gap is largely sustained by overseas rentals of Nvidia chips and knowledge distillation from American models—once America closes both routes, the real gap would be much wider than it appears.
item.content:encoded:
Chinese models lag American ones by about six months, but this gap is largely sustained by overseas rentals of Nvidia chips and knowledge distillation from American models—once America closes both routes, the real gap would be much wider than it appears.

A breakdown of where the six-month gap comes from: rental loopholes, distillation arbitrage, and security gaps—far denser information than generic talk of "US-China AI race."

0:00 DeepSeek's shock was misread as catching up
After DeepSeek's release, Marc Andreessen called it AI's "satellite moment," and Nvidia's market value dropped nearly 600 billion USD in a single day—the largest single-day decline in US stock history. But nearly two years later, China's best models still lag America's best models by roughly six months, while US AI computing capacity is about 16 times that of China. The real question isn't ‘has China caught up’ but how China can be only six months behind given such a vast disparity in computing power.

4:57 Two physical bottlenecks choke China's chip development
The most advanced AI chips depend on two things: ASML, the only company that makes cutting-edge lithography equipment, and specialized high-speed memory. Since 2019, the US has worked with the Netherlands to ban China from importing the most advanced lithography machines; in December 2024 it also banned the required memory, leaving Huawei with only about 16% of its AI chips this year using Chinese-made memory, the rest relying on stockpiles, smuggling, or inferior substitutes. Combined, US computing capacity reaches about 50 times China's—export controls are working.

7:50 The biggest loophole is renting, not selling
America banned Nvidia from selling its most advanced chips to Chinese companies, but didn't ban Chinese companies from renting the same chips at overseas data centers. Tencent rents top-tier chips from Oracle; ByteDance runs Nvidia clusters in Norway; but the largest concentration of rentals is in Malaysia and Singapore. In 2025, four Chinese engineers flew to Malaysia, rented about 300 servers packed with Nvidia chips, and when network speeds proved too slow, they loaded training data into 15 hard drives, packed them in luggage, and flew back to train models at home.

9:23 Those shouting 'every month matters' push faster chip sales
Huang Renxun (黄仁勋) warned that ‘China is only a few nanoseconds behind America,’ while simultaneously advocating for selling more Nvidia chips to China. Trump's former AI czar David Sacks said ‘every month matters,’ yet while in office pushed to loosen restrictions on Nvidia overseas sales. The New York Times found he holds stakes in 449 AI-related companies; the exemption granted to him came from White House counsel itself—signed just one month after Trump fired the head of the independent ethics office. Those shouting loudest about the ‘race’ are often those most hoping chips keep flowing to China.

10:51 Distillation copies most capabilities with one-tenth the effort
Chinese labs massively query top American models, recording answers and reasoning, then train their own models to mimic them—this is distillation. Anthropic reported that in just three months, Alibaba exchanged over 151 million messages with Claude. The Institute for Progress estimates distillation erased roughly half the gap between US and Chinese models, equivalent to freely giving Chinese AI companies four times the computing power. To block distillation requires identifying vast numbers of fake accounts; in one operation, DeepSeek, Moonshot AI (月之暗面), and MiniMax collectively deployed about 24,000 accounts.

12:07 China's AI leaders admit they're far behind
At a Beijing conference in January, Lin Junyang (林俊旸), then technical lead for Alibaba's Qwen, put the odds of Chinese AI companies overtaking top American ones within three to five years at under 20%, calling this ‘quite optimistic’—the reason being computing power gaps. Tang Jie (唐杰), chief AI scientist at Zhipu (智谱), was more pessimistic, arguing that since many of America's best models aren't public, the gap may actually be widening. People sitting at the center of the table don't think their odds are good.

13:47 China plays a different race—deployment, not frontier models
China's goal isn't to build the smartest chatbot but to embed AI in every factory, hospital, and government office, and in this race China has real advantages: US data centers may face a 44-gigawatt power shortfall by 2028, equivalent to needing the grid to absorb California's worth of capacity in just over a year, while China plans to add nearly six times as much generating capacity over the next five years. Last year China installed about 354,000 industrial robots, 59% of the global total; in the first half of this year, 97% of all humanoid robots globally came from Chinese companies.

21:26 Top AI models defend only at level 2 or 3
The industry measures model theft protection on a scale of 1 to 5, with 5 meaning it can withstand the world's top intelligence agencies, but current best estimates show top American AI companies only reach 2 to 3, with plans to hit 5 by 2028 or 2029, and entirely voluntary—unlike nuclear power plants with mandatory federal safety standards. Former Google engineer Linwei Ding was convicted of stealing Google's AI supercomputing architecture and simultaneously working secretly for two Chinese tech companies. If a top model or its training methods are stolen, the window America wins through computing power and export controls could be erased overnight.

item.title: ChatGPT and Claude are the new operating systems, but the moat is not in the interface
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-11-10-a16z-chatgpt和claude已是新操作系统-但护城河不在界面/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-11-10-a16z-chatgpt和claude已是新操作系统-但护城河不在界面/
item.description: HubSpot's co-founder says models are becoming interchangeable infrastructure; no one will strangle entrepreneurs' supply chains. The real moat is accumulated workflows and data, not the chat interface users enter.
item.content:encoded:
HubSpot's co-founder says models are becoming interchangeable infrastructure; no one will strangle entrepreneurs' supply chains. The real moat is accumulated workflows and data, not the chat interface users enter.

The founder gives concrete examples on idea validation, platform ecosystem lessons, and architectural rebuilding; the first 20 minutes cover general startup methodology and can be skipped up to the interface discussion.

7:18 Startup ideas' quality can only be validated, not analyzed beforehand
Dharmesh says the common founder mistake is thinking detailed market analysis (he jokes, ‘eighteen columns in an Excel spreadsheet’) can predict whether an idea will work. But it's almost impossible to know an idea's quality or success probability beforehand. The only way is to build it fast and test it in the market. Even after success, the validated product often looks nothing like the original vision, retaining only ‘genetic’ similarities from the concept. Conclusion: whoever iterates fastest and learns cheapest wins long-term.

17:40 Breaking the ‘do one thing’ rule because customers fear fragmentation
HubSpot launched with content management, SEO, landing pages, forms—an entire marketing toolkit—violating the startup rule to master one thing. Dharmesh explains it wasn't greed: customers' real pain wasn't a missing feature but being overwhelmed and terrified by incompatible tools. The only solution was an ‘all-in-one’ package—a principle HubSpot kept for 20 years: first understand the customer's core problem, then define the product boundary.

20:41 Open platforms eventually close; Twitter is the cautionary tale
Fifteen years ago, early Twitter was radically open—APIs spawned hundreds of third-party clients and companies—but Twitter gradually tightened and turned hostile to developers, shutting down products relying on its ecosystem. Dharmesh says it's not unique to Twitter but a platform disease: eventually platforms deliberately or accidentally crush the developers they cultivated. HubSpot's response: intentionally practice radical transparency with partners, saying upfront what it won't build.

23:54 How to spot a dangerous startup idea: add the word ‘yet’ and see if it still holds
Simple test: if your startup thesis is ‘ChatGPT can't do this yet’ or ‘Claude Cowork can't do that yet’—and the claim still holds after the ‘yet’—it's a red flag because frontier labs will probably patch it soon. Second common mistake: comparing products, not companies. ChatGPT can't do it now, but that doesn't mean OpenAI can't ever. Safe ground is where frontier model companies face structural constraints (regulation) or incentive constraints (not worth their effort).

28:14 In 2023 he feared model companies would strangle startups; now he doesn't
In 2023 Dharmesh's rule was ‘never compete with Sam Altman’—he felt frontier model companies held an unteachable ‘magic formula’ and controlled supply-chain chokepoints. But he says that was wrong. Now models are becoming infrastructure: price and replaceability trend toward commodity. Tools like Open Router make model switching easy. Startups won't be strangled by any one company. Building AI-native now is actually less scary than in 2023.

32:17 ChatGPT and Claude are the new browsers; the interface isn't the endpoint
Take Uber Eats: the app itself isn't complex; the real value is restaurant partnerships and delivery logistics. Same with most B2B software—the interface is just how users do work, not the value itself. ChatGPT and Claude Cowork play the browser role: Google didn't monopolize the application layer; countless software companies thrived ‘running in the browser.’ Same now: companies like HubSpot stay as plugins and connectors plugged into this new ‘operating system’ instead of being replaced.

40:26 Use agentic coding to replay your codebase's architectural history
A newly possible operation: HubSpot has 20 years of GitHub history and complete evaluation sets. Spend, say, $200k in tokens to have AI rewind and replay an architectural decision—assume you'd picked a different data structure or framework back then, rewrite that part, validate with existing evals whether the new version truly optimizes quality, latency, cost. Incumbent companies can now cheaply answer ‘what if we'd chosen differently’—turning legacy weight into testable assets.

49:38 The solo founder wave is usePot's real market soil
U.S. Census Bureau data: new company registrations hit historic highs—2025 saw approximately 5.6 million, 2026 through August surpassed 4 million, with no slowdown. Critically: the bureau predicts whether new companies will hire in two years. Those staying one-person for two years now exceed 70% and keep rising. This is the real market HubSpot Next's solo CRM usePot (launched 30 days ago) targets.

item.title: Revolut CEO likens bank lending to selling options: collect a decade's rent, lose it in one year
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-11-10-cheekypint-revolut-ceo-把银行信贷类比卖期权-收十年租金-一年亏光/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-11-10-cheekypint-revolut-ceo-把银行信贷类比卖期权-收十年租金-一年亏光/
item.description: Lending profits are wiped out by economic cycles, so Revolut keeps lending under 10% of assets, securitizes the rest, and prefers to be a subscription tech company rather than a traditional net-interest-margin bank.
item.content:encoded:
Lending profits are wiped out by economic cycles, so Revolut keeps lending under 10% of assets, securitizes the rest, and prefers to be a subscription tech company rather than a traditional net-interest-margin bank.

See how a new-bank CEO deploys options thinking to reject traditional lending and quantified product elimination to drive rapid growth—information density is high, and the middle section is most valuable.

1:35 Revolut's first seven years had zero growth budget
Storonsky says he never deliberately pursued rapid expansion, only constantly refined the product and solved problems end-to-end. Daily new customer growth climbed from single digits to hundreds to thousands, driven entirely by word of mouth and PR. The company set a formal growth budget for the first time in 2022, began measuring customer payback periods and lifetime value, and launched referral marketing products—the prior seven years had been pure organic growth.

6:24 New product validation turns on unit economics, not creativity
Storonsky says 90% of new ideas will make money if loaded onto the existing customer base, since team costs are far below customer lifetime value, so most ideas don't need strict validation. But real exceptions exist: Revolut launched Revolut Lite, an unlicensed cross-border payment product in 100+ countries, betting on low-cost organic growth. It didn't grow, forcing a shift to paid marketing, and the unit economics didn't work out, so it was killed.

16:24 Lending is like selling options: collect a decade's rent, lose it in one year
Storonsky believes every loan requires a reserve provision, and reserve size depends heavily on macroeconomic variables like unemployment. If unemployment rises from 3% to 6%, book profits could evaporate or flip negative overnight. Subscription businesses only face customer churn in downturns, not negative profit. This is why tech businesses typically trade at 40-50x PE while bank businesses trade at 10x PE. Revolut caps lending at under 10% of the balance sheet and securitizes everything else.

19:51 Products race by launch cohort; bottom performers get defunded
The company has accumulated historical data on roughly 100 new products and tracks each product's gross margin curve by month-of-launch cohort. Top 25th percentile products get team expansions, growing from one team to two, three, four. Bottom 25th percentile products lose funding and staff get reassigned. Storonsky says he's almost never seen a slow-starter turn around later—the first 12 months' trajectory nearly always holds, and that's the main basis for the company's investment decisions.

21:04 An LLM customer manager lives inside the cross-sell engine
Machine learning models score users based on transaction events and where they shop. For example, if a user lands in Ireland and buys an Airalo data plan, they get pushed Revolut's eSIM product. On top of that sits an LLM layer that acts like a real customer manager, weighing all candidate recommendations while balancing the ‘negative value of interruption,’ and decides when, to whom, and what product to recommend—the entire flow runs automatically, so Revolut essentially has no traditional distribution problem.

30:07 Capture under-18 users and they naturally become lifelong customers
Revolut builds products specifically for minors. Once children become ‘Revolut natives,’ switching to an adult account at 18 faces far less friction than pulling adult customers away from traditional banks. Across nearly every European market, Revolut penetration among under-35 is now over 50%, but those 50, 60, 70 and older hold most of the liquid assets and are nearly impossible to migrate from traditional banking.

34:12 AI could halve team sizes, but org structure isn't ready
Storonsky believes one engineer can now handle front-end, back-end, and data science simultaneously, so in theory a two-person team could match an eight-person team's output. But Revolut still organizes permissions and workflows by specialty—iOS, Android, back-end, data science—so it's hard for one person to get full system access and use AI to ship all code. His strategy is to keep running the old framework for now while experimenting with new approaches on the side, then switch once validated.

40:53 Entering America means head-to-head competition with Amex and Chase
The US has historically been stingy with new bank licenses, and most players using bank partnership models have failed—fintech teams and bank compliance teams are essentially two companies forced together, with mismatched cultures and systems. Revolut chose to get its own license and has received conditional OCC approval, targeting remaining approvals next year. Entering the US requires a credit-card-driven product offering benefits at least as good as Amex or Chase, plus Revolut-exclusive lines like wealth management and crypto trading.

item.title: The more secular politics becomes, the more it resembles a holy war
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-11-10-goodfight-政治变得越世俗-反而越像一场圣战/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-11-10-goodfight-政治变得越世俗-反而越像一场圣战/
item.description: Two authors argue that when people stop deriving identity and ultimate meaning from religion, this longing does not disappear but instead transfers into politics—which is the root cause of American politics becoming ‘holy war-like’.
item.content:encoded:
Two authors argue that when people stop deriving identity and ultimate meaning from religion, this longing does not disappear but instead transfers into politics—which is the root cause of American politics becoming ‘holy war-like’.

Starting from the theory that ‘politics is becoming religious,’ it eventually lands in specific debates within the Democratic Party about the authenticity of faith candidates; the second half's case analysis offers higher value and is worth hearing through to the end.

0:00 Politics is filling the spiritual void left by religion
Kaemingk's argument is that democratic theorists long believed secularization would make people more rational and unified, but American reality contradicts this: as religious identity declines, political polarization rises instead. The reason is that people no longer derive identity and meaning from religion, instead seeking them from political tribal identity—who are good and who are bad, the ultimate meaning of life, all concentrated in elections and parties. This produces political language imbued with apocalyptic sense like ‘this is the most important election of our lifetime,’ with politics itself beginning to perform functions that should belong to religion.

0:00 Monotheism's true function is pulling politics off the pedestal
The three believe monotheism's greatest contribution to democracy is not moral doctrine but ‘desacralizing politics’—pulling presidents, parties, and particular elections down from ultimate status. Kaemingk raises the ancient concept of ‘idolatry,’ which actually carries urgent contemporary political significance: placing ordinary things in life (an election, a political figure) on a sacred pedestal is itself a political danger. Judaism, Islam, and Christianity share a common legacy of reminding people never to treat any secular thing as the source of ultimate salvation.

0:00 Belief in the afterlife paradoxically relaxes political intensity
The book has a dedicated chapter called ‘In Defense of Hell,’ arguing that belief in the afterlife's judgment brings a kind of political relief—you need not make final reckoning with every dictator and injustice in this life, because there will eventually be a final accounting. Hamid argues this is not defending political passivity, but rather that it allows people to avoid the obsession with ‘must completely win in this lifetime,’ and thus handle politics more lightly. Conversely, the 20th century's most destructive communist movements were precisely secular ideologies attempting to realize paradise on earth.

0:00 Secular ideology killed more people in the 20th century than religious war did
Against the common accusation that ‘religion is the cause of violence,’ Hamid counters that the 20th century itself was a century when secular ideologies killed tens of millions—Mao's Cultural Revolution and the anti-Christian core of Nazism are examples. Both acknowledge that religious extremism has existed historically (from Christian religious wars to Islamic extremist organizations), but they argue that secular ideology in the modern era often escapes the same scrutiny, and Mounk agrees this has been underestimated.

0:00 European religious wars were power struggles, not conflicts over faith
Kaemingk cites William Cavanaugh's “The Myth of Religious Violence” to point out that conflicts historically called ‘religious wars’ in European history were largely different power brokers exploiting tensions between Catholicism and Protestantism to serve their political and economic ends, with religion being more a manipulated tool than the root of conflict. This stands opposite the historical narrative often invoked by secularists to argue that ‘religion cannot enter public life.’

0:00 Party identity is now replacing race as the most dangerous dividing line
Mounk raises that the most dangerous division today is no longer primarily race or class, but party identity—polls show American parents are more likely to be unhappy if their child marries someone from the opposite party than if they marry someone of a different race. Religion could originally have been a ‘bridging identity’ across parties: Catholicism, some Protestant churches, and Islam in America are all highly multiethnic and could reasonably connect people in different parties. But in reality religion has become highly mapped onto party division—observant white people are likely Republican, secular white progressives are likely Democratic.

0:00 Democratic Muslim candidates are selected to be too smooth
Kaemingk criticizes Democratic Muslim candidates like Zohran: they align perfectly with Democratic positions on gender and sexual orientation, with no genuinely ‘strange’ Muslim perspectives. What he hopes to see is a Muslim elected with openly orthodox Islamic positions (such as diverging from party mainstream on gender issues) rather than being treated as symbolic packaging. Hamid partly agrees, suggesting Abdul El-Sayed may privately hold more conservative views but chooses to avoid them for fear of angering the progressive base; he also notes that the Democratic Party was not inherently meant to be secular—four or five decades ago in the Jimmy Carter era, it still accommodated large numbers of white evangelicals.

item.title: Musk's product algorithm: automation is the final step, not the first
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-11-10-knowledge-马斯克的产品算法-自动化是最后一步-不是第一步/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-11-10-knowledge-马斯克的产品算法-自动化是最后一步-不是第一步/
item.description: Tesla's team got stuck on the same problem for months by automating first. Musk's algorithm instead demands: cut requirements, simplify the process, run it manually until it works—automation is always the last step.
item.content:encoded:
Tesla's team got stuck on the same problem for months by automating first. Musk's algorithm instead demands: cut requirements, simplify the process, run it manually until it works—automation is always the last step.

For founders and product managers seeking concrete operating mechanisms, not leadership platitudes. Every case is specific and actionable.

1:03 Musk evaluates people by solving real problems with them
McNeill's first meeting with Musk had no small talk. Musk brought him directly to the factory floor to walk the Model X production line. Through consecutive questions, they discovered that workers had to install Falcon Wing door bolts by reaching underneath the car where they couldn't see. McNeill proposed a fixture; the factory built it that same night. Musk's standard for hiring isn't experience or credentials, but this: ‘If we had the same information, would we reach the same answer?’

4:09 He made a major decision for Musk before even officially joining
McNeill investigated Tesla's biggest problem before joining: they'd promised to sell 12,000 cars that quarter, but had only sold 3,000 after a month and a half. He anonymously test-drove at eight stores and got no follow-ups at any. He discovered that over the past 30 days, about 10,000 test-drivers had been left with no follow-up. The root cause: Tesla had no commission structure, so salespeople had no incentive to close deals. Without authorization, he ordered a global halt to new test-drive assignments until salespeople completed follow-ups with existing prospects. When he called to apologize to Musk for overstepping his authority, Musk was silent for nearly a minute, then said it was a good decision.

13:58 Making salespeople push hard without commissions
Musk refuses commissions because he wants the store experience to be the exact opposite of a traditional car dealership. The team's solution: hang a leaderboard in each store ranking monthly sales, with a line drawn seemingly arbitrarily through the middle, and never explain what the line means. Without spending a dollar on bonuses, salespeople still fight to stay above the line. ‘Above the line’ became the store's new universal currency.

17:44 Weekly Autopilot updates require not waiting for perfect
Other automakers release updates only once or twice a year, testing every scenario exhaustively. Tesla's approach: push a release as soon as simulation testing reaches sufficient confidence, because waiting six months for maximum safety means deliberately throwing away six months of real-world feedback. McNeill says this transforms a car into a product that appreciates rather than depreciates over time—range, acceleration, and longevity can all improve without replacing the vehicle. This inverts the traditional automaker logic of treating a car as a one-time static product.

44:27 Jobs gave iPod engineers exactly two hard constraints
When designing the iPod, Jobs locked his team in a room for a week until they could answer two things: it must hold 1,000 songs and find any song in 4 seconds. Plus ‘it has to look beautiful.’ When engineers suggested adding FM radio like Samsung, Jobs asked, ‘Is that 1,000 songs or 4 seconds?’ If not, it doesn't happen. To meet those two constraints, the team was forced to invent technologies that didn't yet exist—flash storage and index chips. Much of Musk's later approach to product design comes from this template.

51:40 One-piece casting bought Tesla eight years of manufacturing lead
Doug Field's team demonstrated the solution with a Hot Wheels toy car: replace the car's skeleton of hundreds of robot-welded parts with a single molten aluminum casting in two large pieces. At the time, no one knew how to pour 1,600-degree molten aluminum into such a large mold without it shattering—it was considered physically impossible. Once they achieved it, the factory eliminated nearly half its floor space and welding robots. Tesla leaped years ahead in casting technology, and only now are competitors beginning to catch up.

55:47 Automation only becomes the last step of the algorithm
The book title “The Algorithm” comes from the team's retrospective of past failures. Step one: question and eliminate every non-essential requirement—compress a 12-page loan contract to one paragraph. Step two: redesign the process to include only steps customers will actually pay for. Step three: run the new process manually and refine it. Step four: increase speed to expose weaknesses and failure points. Only after the process runs smoothly does step five arrive: automation. The team admits to the mistake of automating first, which trapped them for months on the same problem with no way out.

1:31:23 Uber and Lyft turned each other into commodities
When McNeill was COO of Lyft, his biggest regret is that both companies went to war on price early on, with identical decals on their cars and riders and drivers treating the two apps as interchangeable. That's the definition of commoditization: when only price is left to compare, even strong brand positioning can't save margins. Both companies were making no money at the gross profit level. If he could do it again, he'd convince founders to build brand premium before price wars start, rather than trying to recover after years of price competition.

item.title: The Forgotten Victorian Strongwomen: When Weight Meant Strength and Beauty
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-11-10-ninepi-被遗忘的维多利亚大力女明星-当年体重大才被认为又强又美/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-11-10-ninepi-被遗忘的维多利亚大力女明星-当年体重大才被认为又强又美/
item.description: The modern ideal of slenderness is only around a hundred years old. In the Victorian era, circus strongwomen weighing two hundred pounds were called ‘the strongest and most beautiful women in the world’.
item.content:encoded:
The modern ideal of slenderness is only around a hundred years old. In the Victorian era, circus strongwomen weighing two hundred pounds were called ‘the strongest and most beautiful women in the world’.

This episode advances through personal narrative without industry insight or actionable takeaways, best for listeners interested in women's sports history or the evolution of fitness culture as story.

2:04 Record holder got no toast at her own celebration
Jan Todd traveled to Scotland to set a record lifting the Denny Stones. At the celebration dinner, the local mayor poured whisky only for the two male weightlifters who'd accompanied her—nothing for Jan. She swallowed her anger that night and attempted twice, failing both times. When she stepped away to collect herself, her husband Terry said, ‘Do this one for the whisky guy.’ She returned and lifted both stones successfully. The pattern was clear: even when a woman set the record, the recognition and toasts went to the men around her.

6:09 Pseudoscience measured strength by race, not body alone
In the 1890s, American medicine promoted false theory: women's body energy was finite, reserved for reproduction. Any exertion—exercise, reading, even politics—would drain reproductive energy and cause ‘hysteria’. On its surface, medical concern; in practice, it enshrined women's weakness as natural law. But this theory applied only to white, affluent women. Black women, assigned generations of heavy physical labor, were described by the same pseudoscience as ‘naturally tireless and pain-free,’ making their strength not a violation of nature but a justification for exploitation. The boundary of feminine frailty shifted by race.

9:11 Fitness marketed to women only as marriage maintenance
In the 1950s, Jack LaLanne opened one of America's first public gyms and trained people with disabilities and seniors in weightlifting—genuinely progressive for the era. But on television, facing stay-at-home mothers as his daytime audience, his pitch changed. He aired a ‘fan letter’ from a woman whose body had changed: her husband wanted divorce, her children were ashamed to bring friends home, her friends had abandoned her. The show reframed exercise as a tool to save marriages and restore dignity—not as a woman's own path to strength. For women, fitness had only one permitted entrance: looking good enough not to be abandoned.

19:21 No women's sport existed, so she invented it
Jan's first time in a gym, she casually tried 225 pounds and lifted it easily. Her husband Terry, a former national champion in both weightlifting and powerlifting, recognized immediately that she was ‘perfectly leveraged for the squat’—he proposed she chase world records. The idea was almost absurd, but not because she lacked strength. The infrastructure didn't exist: no women's bodybuilding, no women's weightlifting, no women's Olympic lifting competitions. Every record Jan would later break had no precedent, no rules, no judging standards—she and Terry had to invent each one from zero. She didn't race down an existing track; she built it first.

23:23 Circus strongwomen were already breaking records before Jan was born
A deceased circus strongman named Otley Coulter left 380 boxes of personal archives. When Jan and Terry bought and sorted through them, they found magazines and letters from the late 1800s onward, documenting female circus performers named Sandwina and Vulcana lifting anvils, horses, even their own husbands. Jan had believed she was the first woman to lift heavy objects; the media reported it that way. But the archives revealed a different history: decades before Jan's birth, professional women strongmen called ‘the strongest and most beautiful women in the world’ made their living from strength and lived with economic security. They weren't forgotten by history; they were erased from it.

26:24 Thinness as beauty is barely a hundred years old
Jan kept returning to a puzzle: Victorian-era doctors warned women that bicycling would scar their faces and prolapse their uteruses, yet those same-era circus strongwomen were simultaneously celebrated as both ‘the strongest’ and ‘the most beautiful.’ Her conclusion: the aesthetic standard itself was different then. People didn't consider thinness beautiful; greater weight signaled health and prosperity, not excess. Strength and beauty weren't competing qualities in that era—they only became opposed after slenderness culture took hold and redefined what counts as strong and what counts as feminine as opposites.

28:24 The same drive that breaks records also beats cancer
At 36, Jan was diagnosed with ovarian cancer. The doctor was direct: survival rates at that stage were roughly 25 percent. Driving home, Terry told her, ‘When have you ever been outside the top 25%?’ That sentence, Jan says, sustained her through treatment. She survived. The price was that she and Terry would never have biological children—that possibility was gone. They redirected the energy they'd set aside for raising a next generation into building an archive. That archive became the Stark Center, now the world's largest repository of weightlifting and sports culture history.

33:26 We still don't know how strong women can be
At the episode's end, Jan distills strength training to one principle: progressive overload—find a weight that genuinely challenges you, train until it no longer does, then add more. The body grows stronger by repeatedly facing what it cannot yet do. The specific number is irrelevant; what counts as heavy is relative to the lifter. She adds a historical perspective: men have always had the unquestioned default right to be strong. Women have had explicit permission to run fast or become strong for perhaps 50 years. So when asked what women's ceiling for strength is, her standard answer is: we don't yet know.

item.title: Theodore Roosevelt didn't create the NCAA; a campus death did
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-11-10-throughline-老罗斯福不是ncaa诞生的真正推手-一场校园死亡才是导火索/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-11-10-throughline-老罗斯福不是ncaa诞生的真正推手-一场校园死亡才是导火索/
item.description: After 1905's ‘death harvest’, the NCAA's rules committee came from the NYU president bypassing the Big Three, not from Roosevelt's conference.
item.content:encoded:
After 1905's ‘death harvest’, the NCAA's rules committee came from the NYU president bypassing the Big Three, not from Roosevelt's conference.

One core reversal: the NCAA's true architect wasn't Theodore Roosevelt but an inter-university power struggle.

8:17 The flying wedge transplanted military tactics directly to the field
Without forward-pass rules, 1870s football became pure collision. Offenses formed a V-shaped flying wedge—one player at the point, teammates behind using collective force to drive him forward. The tactic borrowed its name directly from military wedge-charge formations. Head protection was minimal—just long hair and a wool cap. Defense meant launching another group of bodies into collision.

9:22 Football became combat training to preserve young men's military fitness
After the Civil War, America's economy shifted from agriculture to commerce, raising fears that young men would lose combat readiness. Football filled the void: it demanded obedience, teamwork, strength, and courage—military virtues. The sport's violence wasn't accidental; society actively encouraged it.

10:25 Nineteen players died in 1905, defining college football's deadliest year
In 1905, roughly 19 people died in college football games—including high schoolers and amateurs, not just college players—while 137 suffered serious injuries. The San Francisco Call documented the causes: 4 deaths from internal collision injuries, 6 from concussions, 3 from spinal damage, plus 19 skull fractures. This toll drove every subsequent reform.

12:31 Theodore Roosevelt's White House summit produced no rule changes
Roosevelt, a football enthusiast whose son was injured in 1905, brought Harvard, Princeton, and Yale presidents to the White House to demand safer play. Historian Eric Moyen called it a ‘nothing burger’: the three dominant programs had no incentive to change rules that would help rivals compete. A month passed with no action.

14:32 The real reform catalyst was a player's death at Thanksgiving
A player's death at Thanksgiving 1905 in an NYU-Union College game pushed NYU's president to act. He sent a telegram to Harvard's president demanding a new meeting; when refused, he bypassed the Big Three, convened every college president with a football team, and they established the rules committee that became the NCAA.

15:33 Forward-pass legalization was designed to break up mass collisions
The committee swiftly changed the rules: first-down advancement moved from 5 to 10 yards, and the forward pass became legal in 1906. The goal was clear—disperse players across the field to catch passes instead of forming solid lines for head-on collision. This was the crisis's most direct technical legacy.

16:36 The NCAA fought over money and power from its founding
Despite the safety crisis driving its creation, the committee was ‘never just about safety’, according to historian Eric Moyen. It debated payment for players, their name-and-image rights (the precursor to NIL), academic standards for athletes, and—most crucially—who enforces the rules: the NCAA, individual universities, or coaches. These exact issues resurfaced virtually unchanged a century later.

18:40 Today's NIL chaos echoes the 1905 power vacuum exactly
The confusion around NIL, transfer portals, and coaching salaries directly mirrors 1905, according to Moyen: then, university presidents negotiated safety rules among themselves; now, leagues and coaches must negotiate money and authority instead. Same power vacuum, different stakes. The NCAA declined to comment. No clear answer exists yet.

item.title: Many historical hauntings were actually carbon monoxide poisoning
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-11-10-tpwky-历史上许多-闹鬼事件-其实是一氧化碳中毒/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-11-10-tpwky-历史上许多-闹鬼事件-其实是一氧化碳中毒/
item.description: Carbon monoxide not only outcompetes oxygen for hemoglobin, but also prevents already-bound oxygen from being released — this dual mechanism produces symptoms so bizarre they were historically mistaken for hauntings or mental illness.
item.content:encoded:
Carbon monoxide not only outcompetes oxygen for hemoglobin, but also prevents already-bound oxygen from being released — this dual mechanism produces symptoms so bizarre they were historically mistaken for hauntings or mental illness.

Clarifies CO poisoning's physiology and misdiagnosis history; also covers why household CO detectors are essential. Information density: moderate-to-high.

4:20 Carbon monoxide poisoning is often misdiagnosed as hauntings or psychiatric illness
A Reddit user received sticky notes in unfamiliar handwriting reminding them to do tasks, yet had no memory of writing them, plus severe headaches. Someone suggested not a ghost or the landlord, but CO poisoning causing confusion and memory loss. A detector read 100 ppm. The hosts stress that CO poisoning's worst aspect is that the brain doesn't suspect it immediately—instead it invents other explanations.

12:40 Hemoglobin's affinity for carbon monoxide is over 200 times that of oxygen
Oxygen depends on hemoglobin as a "transport truck" throughout the body. CO outcompetes oxygen for binding—with over 200 times higher affinity. Worse, CO left-shifts the oxygen dissociation curve, making hemoglobin reluctant to release already-bound oxygen. Dual strike: hemoglobin binds less oxygen and releases less oxygen. Tissues become hypoxic.

25:55 Between 10 and 40 percent of CO survivors develop delayed neuropsychiatric symptoms
Between 10 and 40 percent of CO survivors develop delayed neuropsychiatric symptoms: depression, Parkinsonian features, dementia, psychosis. Medicine doesn't know who gets it, why, or whether dose or duration matters. This is why emergency departments often misdiagnose chronic CO exposure as a psychiatric episode.

26:58 The only treatment for carbon monoxide poisoning is oxygen
No drug can metabolize carboxyhemoglobin; the only treatment is high-concentration oxygen to displace CO from hemoglobin. At normal oxygen levels, CO has a 4-6 hour half-life in blood; pure oxygen (100%) reduces this to 40-80 minutes; hyperbaric oxygen further reduces it to 15-30 minutes. However, not all hospitals have hyperbaric facilities.

41:18 Science magazine exposed a Boston haunting as CO poisoning in 1913
MIT researcher Franz Schneider Jr. was asked to investigate a Boston "haunted" apartment. Residents felt held down at night, paralyzed, saw hallucinations; children were lethargic by day and hard to wake; previous tenants reported identical symptoms—apparently proving the house was cursed. Schneider found an "extremely defective hot air furnace" leaking CO. Nearly identical cases appeared in a 1921 ophthalmology journal article.

46:23 Coal mine canaries detected danger 20 minutes before human collapse
Birds' respiratory systems extract oxygen far more efficiently than mammals, making them highly sensitive to gaseous toxins like CO. They fell from their perches about 20 minutes before humans lost consciousness. After a Welsh mining disaster in 1894, J.S. Haldane formally recommended deploying canaries in mines, though people had used them since the early 1800s. Miners had deep affection for the birds and maintained specialized revival boxes. The practice continued until the 1980s, when electronic detectors replaced them.

51:40 Intentional US CO deaths outnumber accidental deaths by 5 to 10 times
The US experiences approximately 600 accidental CO deaths per year. Intentional deaths—predominantly suicide—are 5 to 10 times higher, reaching up to 15,000 annually. A 2017 study estimated roughly 50,000 CO poisoning cases in the US yearly, with a 1-3% mortality rate. Globally, low- and middle-income countries see significantly higher rates of CO poisoning and death because coal and wood don't burn completely.

54:48 The body naturally produces carbon monoxide; now scientists want it as medicine
Normal hemoglobin metabolism produces trace amounts of CO naturally. Scientists realized low-dose CO might work like nitric oxide—acting as a vasodilator, regulating inflammation, possibly functioning as a neurotransmitter. Slow-inhalation formulations are now in phase 1 clinical trials for vascular and inflammatory diseases. But administration methods and precise targeting remain in early-stage exploration.

item.title: Teach kids to lie for safety rather than risk harm
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-11-10-asklisa-心理学家-教孩子对同伴撒谎自保-好过逞强说真话/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-11-10-asklisa-心理学家-教孩子对同伴撒谎自保-好过逞强说真话/
item.category: Ask Lisa: The Psychology of Raising Tweens & Teens
item.description: When peers pressure kids to smoke weed or similar, she'd rather teach them to lie and blame their parents to escape, rather than let them risk it because they can't find a dignified way to say no—safety first, not honesty above all.
item.content:encoded:
When peers pressure kids to smoke weed or similar, she'd rather teach them to lie and blame their parents to escape, rather than let them risk it because they can't find a dignified way to say no—safety first, not honesty above all.

Entirely Q&A format, no new theory but many usable scripts. For parents solving conflicts, not attending lectures.

3:05 Most lies aren't born from bad intent
She sorts children's lying into three categories: hiding wrongdoing, avoiding responsibility, or protecting privacy. The privacy type is most often misread by parents—when a child doesn't volunteer details like which park they visited, they're exercising normal developmental autonomy, not lying, but parents interpret it as deception: 'why would you lie about something so small?'

6:12 Teach kids to lie for safety rather than risk harm
At a party, if someone offers weed, teach your kid a safe lie like 'my parents do random drug tests'—it doesn't have to be true. She'd rather kids escape with a kind lie than be pressured into risk because they lack a dignified refusal. Safety first; honesty is a later conversation.

11:21 What kids firmly believe as true often isn't actually true
When a child sincerely describes events that contradict your reality, don't deny them outright. She says: 'the same event looks different from different angles.' If they persist, play 'the perspective game'—you fully state their case, they fully state yours. Often advances the conversation better than debating facts.

15:34 Stop asking if they did it—just name what you both know
Quoting child psychologist Haim Ginott: skip the trap question 'were you there?' Just say 'we both know that's not true.' Then ask 'why didn't you tell me'—shift from catching them to understanding the lie.

19:52 When they say 'I don't know' why they lied, believe them
When kids say 'I don't know why I lied,' they likely mean it—they haven't worked it out themselves. Don't push. Say: 'This is hard, let's talk tomorrow.' Emphasize: 'You're good, lying bothers you too.' Come back the next day.

23:58 Tie freedom to honesty, not lifetime distrust to a lie
Don't say 'if you lie again I'll never trust you'—it blocks redemption. Instead: link freedom to trustworthiness. A lie means their freedom quota drops now. As they rebuild trust through honesty, freedom returns gradually. Trust is not a death sentence; it rises and falls with their choices.

26:01 Model honesty yourself before you demand it from your kids
Two checks: Are you honest? Kids sense hypocrisy immediately. Second: have you ever punished honesty or hit harder after a confession? If so, apologize. Tell them your past reactions made it harder for them to tell the truth.

item.title: Stop Rushing to Pull Kids Apart: Conflict Itself Is How They Learn Social Skills
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-11-10-unruffled-孩子打架别急着拉开-冲突本身就是他们在学社交/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-11-10-unruffled-孩子打架别急着拉开-冲突本身就是他们在学社交/
item.description: Frequent yelling, biting, even slapping you—often doesn't signal a broken child, but rather what happens when parents intervene: conflict becomes a competition for ‘Mom's attention’.
item.content:encoded:
Frequent yelling, biting, even slapping you—often doesn't signal a broken child, but rather what happens when parents intervene: conflict becomes a competition for ‘Mom's attention’.

No new research or data, but Janet offers a concrete, actionable seven-step framework that explains why taking sides, urging peace, or forcibly pulling kids apart actually escalates conflict.

7:17 Both stay in the conflict by choice: it's not one-sided victimhood
The letter writer believed her two-and-a-half-year-old son upset his four-and-a-half-year-old sister through unreasonableness. But Janet notes that conflict almost always goes both ways: if the sister truly didn't want to engage, she could walk away entirely. Both children kept participating in the argument, which reveals they both wanted it on some level—this is precisely how children learn and get to know each other through conflict, not through victim-and-perpetrator relationships.

8:24 When parents intervene, conflict becomes a power struggle with them
What often escalates conflict isn't the children themselves, but parental discomfort with what's happening. Once parents step in, what unfolds between the kids quietly becomes a game of ‘who can get Mom to come’—which explains why these squabbles almost always occur within earshot, not when parents are absent. The more parents resist the urge to intervene, the more the conflict stays with the children to resolve themselves.

12:44 Younger children's provocative moves are usually bids for connection
Janet challenges the assumption that younger children are always innocent victims. Frequently, it's the younger child who deliberately starts the conflict—even infants who can only crawl know which toy to reach for to provoke older siblings. Because they prefer any interaction to complete disconnection, they'd rather be yelled at than ignored. Understanding this, parents stop reducing conflict to ‘who started it’.

13:44 Set the agreement before conflict: resolve it yourselves, I come if you call
Janet suggests having a conversation during a calm moment, not during conflict. Tell your children that you've noticed them yelling, biting, and hitting; you've been rushing in to make decisions for them, but now you want to give that back—you'll only step in if they actively call for ‘Mom, help me’. This advance conversation establishes their capacity to handle conflicts far better than intervening in the moment.

17:55 If you do intervene, there's only one rule: neutrality, always
If the children actually call you in, Janet's core principle is absolute neutrality: don't speak for either side, don't judge who's right or wrong, don't take a team. She stresses this is harder than simply deciding who's at fault, but this kind of impartiality lets them feel you love both equally, rather than becoming one more judge in their lives.

18:57 Stop the hit without removing the child: less intervention is better
When physical intervention is needed, Janet's advice is ‘do the smallest, most effective thing’—block with your hand, hold their wrist—not pick them up and carry them away. Picking up and removing appears more decisive, but it sends the message ‘this is a serious problem that must be stopped immediately’, leaving the child feeling cast as either the perpetrator or the victim. In the letter, when the mother picked up her son, he slapped her face—exactly the kind of backlash that comes from overintervening.

23:59 Explaining one child to another isn't reassurance, it's insecurity
Citing Siblings Without Rivalry, Janet explains why the mother's comment—‘he's only two’—fails to console the older sister. That kind of remark frames the sister as more mature and capable, seeming to side with her, but it actually reveals that she too could be dismissed or compared based on age at any time. It plants anxiety, not real safety or connection.

26:01 Light-touch parenting isn't the same as tolerating abuse
To the common pushback—‘I was beaten by my older brother and my parents never did anything’—Janet separates ‘trusting kids and intervening when necessary’ from ‘total abandonment’. She points out that the child who habitually bullies siblings is usually the one who has absorbed the deepest parental rejection and judgment; that displaced pain gets redirected at siblings. Parents maintaining neutrality with both children—genuine impartiality rather than indifference—is what breaks the cycle.
