item.content:encoded:
Xiaoteng argues that big tech companies' problem isn't insufficient chips or money, but financial statements that force management to convert lab research into products. This centripetal force makes breakthrough innovation unlikely to happen inside big companies, yet they still make steady money by trading compute for equity or partnerships.

If you're deciding whether to bet on big-company AI labs or startup model teams, this episode explains the structural incentives rather than offering empty cheerleading.

4:00 Jump out at 90 percent to explore something new
He roots this in RL's exploration-exploitation tradeoff: even seemingly wasteful random exploration at 10% is necessary to approach a global optimum. Obsessing over perfecting the current task risks local-maximum lock-in. He acknowledges startups need someone pushing to 100%, so he recruited two co-founders for that work and focuses on exploration himself.

18:10 The gap widens now but Chinese advantages will emerge
He expects the US lead to widen near-term: OpenAI and Anthropic deployed earlier on data and large-scale RL. But he's long-term bullish on two points: Chinese compute infrastructure becomes ‘usable’ next year, and China outmatches the US at organizing and operating on data—many American big companies outsource data cleaning to Chinese workers anyway. The true risk is if OpenAI breaks through on long-chain reasoning (week-scale reasoning, Fields Medal-level proofs) and no one catches up.

22:21 Big companies will collectively lose the model race
He uses Tencent Hunyuan as an example: the team earned exceptional permissions and resources with solid technology, but the parent company's ROI targets decide whether lab output gets commercialized and resources redeployed. He cites “The Cost of Staying”, arguing large companies have inherent centripetal pull against breakthrough innovation. But this doesn't mean they lose commercially: they extract value from startups by trading compute for equity or selling them services.

30:42 Design efficiency unlocks the data volume that matters
His assessment of Chinese models: DeepSeek invested most aggressively in infrastructure and model codesign—shrinking MLA from four channels to one, separating encoder and decoder—achieving dramatically lower training and inference costs, enabling more data and heavier RL training. GLM is pragmatic, with the most complete data pipeline. Kimi favors innovation and gets fancy. Mimax lacks conviction—it built differentiation with Linear Attention but abandoned it, then chased revenue and IPO too early, disrupting model iteration.

37:40 Build the product first; research gaps follow
He attacks NewLab teams for inverting the process: build flashy technology (world models, diffusion, RSI), then hunt for use cases. That's hammers seeking nails. The correct order: ship a product prototype, resist scaling pressure, collect real data, then identify the research needed. To assess whether a NewLab is solid, ask if it has genuinely attempted closing a commercial loop.

45:55 The model is the only differentiator that matters
He observes that in the US, whether companies work on data or infrastructure, middle-tier players almost universally end up building their own models and buying compute. The model is where user experience differs most; frontend and harness don't matter. He compares it to history: people remember great swords but not scabbards; harness is the scabbard. Most people in China who fit this profile haven't updated their thinking; they lack conviction about adopting external RL services.

54:58 Tiny parameter shifts create entirely different model personalities
Constrained to four H800s, Mind Lab pursued LoRA; later research from Thinking Machines validated that LoRA often matches full training. They broke strategy into three: scale up (bigger base), scale down (smaller, faster LoRA), scale out (massive concurrent LoRA). He uses human genetics as analogy: humans differ by less than 0.5% in DNA yet behave completely differently; LoRA works the same way against the base model. By April, they ran a million concurrent LoRA inferences on a single base.

57:21 Models need a lightweight unit for judgment storage
He sees the core gap in current training approaches not in algorithms but storage. AI can read 300+ papers daily, far faster than humans, but lacks a way to compress the judgment formed across 300 papers, store it, and iterate. Real continual learning requires a lightweight, iterable unit to hold that taste-level judgment. That's a direction Ilya is exploring as well.

item.title: How expert credibility collapsed—and now no one can contain AI that might end humanity
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-11-07-goodfight-专家阶层自毁信誉的代价-没人能再管住会-终结人类-的ai/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-11-07-goodfight-专家阶层自毁信誉的代价-没人能再管住会-终结人类-的ai/
item.description: Wolf argues that after populism destroyed expert credibility, even Anthropic's own disclosure of risks like ‘ending humanity’ barely registers.
item.content:encoded:
Wolf argues that after populism destroyed expert credibility, even Anthropic's own disclosure of risks like ‘ending humanity’ barely registers.

The first half explores whether democracy can recover; the second half questions whether AI might eliminate human economic value—the latter carries more insight.

0:00 Democratic restoration has already become impossible
Wolf admits in his book's new preface that he's more pessimistic than when he wrote it. He once believed society would self-correct after seeing populism's damage; now he thinks that once a truly uncontrollable, fully populist government takes power, the damage runs too deep to reverse—not merely ‘weakened’ but ‘destroyed’ in certain dimensions. He cites Poland's president-versus-government standoff as proof that harm becomes irreversible. He also notes that AI and other technological shifts have dismantled the old left-right party structures altogether.

0:00 The template for democracy's future is Argentina, not fascism
Against Mounk's optimism that America self-corrects, Wolf offers a different historical parallel. He used to cite 1930s fascism as his benchmark, but now finds Latin America more instructive. The pattern: authoritarian government seizes power, runs out of resources within years, forced to hold elections; the elected democratic government cannot solve root causes; the cycle repeats. Government never achieves real efficiency because institutions lack stability and personnel lack tenure, yet it stops well short of total dictatorship. Wolf expects Britain, continental Europe, and India to follow this rhythm, with only small wealthy societies—Switzerland, the Netherlands, Nordic countries—likely to escape.

0:00 Dirty democracy's real cost is economic, not moral
Mounk introduces ‘dirty democracy’—where rules are manipulated but competition persists. Wolf adds the economic dimension: such systems impose enormous hidden costs on growth. Functioning economies require decades of long-horizon risk investment, which demands trust in the rule of law, property rights, contract enforcement, stable government services, and predictable trade and currency policy. He concedes the US economy performs well, but credits it not to Trump-era policies but to unsustainable fiscal expansion funding short-term demand, plus an AI boom from technological accumulation that has compressed into this moment.

0:00 When expert credibility collapses, no one can govern AI
Over three decades, the defining political fact is that experts and intellectuals have become the public's enemy—because their recommended policies failed to benefit ordinary people, opening space for populists. Applied to AI: we should have assembled expert panels to seriously evaluate risk, as we did for nuclear weapons fifty years ago. Instead, we cannot organize any genuine discussion. His evidence: Anthropic's IPO—potentially valued in the trillion-dollar range—discloses ‘ending humanity’ as one risk, and the disclosure lands with barely a response. This is learned helplessness taken to its logical extreme.

0:00 If machines think better than humans, what's left for us
Wolf returns to an analogy he uses in his column: horses were once the world's essential technology, now they're entertainment. Humanity's truly scarce capacity is ‘thinking’—not mere intelligence, but thinking applied to everything. If AI and robots excel at thinking, wealthy people would prefer to be surrounded by machines except for their closest family. He half-jokingly wonders whether fewer people having children reflects a deep sense that there's no future for them—but he explicitly states ‘I'm not saying this is true,’ only that the coincidence is curious.

0:00 His nightmare: the morning every bank account on Earth reaches zero
Wolf escalates AI risk from economics to something more urgent. The entire digital economy—banks, power grids, trillions in daily corporate finance—will eventually run on AI. We already see AI companies concede these systems behave capriciously and erratically, spinning out of control. He cites a real incident from that day in Sweden: hackers (possibly an AI bot) infiltrated supermarket freezer systems, raised temperatures until all food spoiled. ‘These look like terrorism.’ His nightmare: one morning the world wakes to find every bank account has been zeroed. The world economy halts. Nothing guarantees it won't happen.

0:00 In the age of AI, all humans become dependent on rents
Wolf sketches an extreme scenario: if AI does nearly all production, most people's marginal labor contribution becomes negative. To preserve ‘humans collectively control their own fate,’ society must radically socialize production, distribution, and exchange—a system no one has seriously designed yet. His analogy: everyone becomes old-time nobility, unproductive but living off land and peasant output. In the AI world, all output flows from AI; a just society must distribute these rents to everyone. People live by consumption rights, not production.

0:00 Without productive work, humans never truly develop into adults
Mounk objects: old nobility actually managed estates, administered peasants, bore inherited duties—essentially running small businesses. Plus their identity drew meaning from rank: ‘I am a Duke’—a slot that cannot exist for everyone. Wolf agrees and deepens it: strip away people's ability to contribute to society through their own effort, and they never truly mature. They remain perpetual children, perpetually cared for. That is not life; it is the world ‘Brave New World’ explores. Both note that scarcity does not vanish: energy, land, ocean views, ‘there can only be one president’—positional goods stay scarce. Marx erred in thinking abolishing property solves distribution; without markets, whoever commands the most force writes the rules.

item.content:encoded:
Hyman says muscle is the decisive asset for avoiding frailty, but today's popular GLP-1 weight-loss drugs cause massive muscle loss while achieving weight loss—and this is the side effect worth really worrying about.

The first half is personal diet logistics with moderate information density; the second half is worth listening to for its discussion of GLP-1's muscle loss, the prevalence of nutritional deficiencies, and the falling cost of testing.

2:04 Muscle is the hard currency of longevity
Hyman drinks an immediate post-strength-training "longevity shake" with roughly 40g whey protein and 5–10g creatine, because muscle loss leads to frailty and functional decline—the mechanism that ultimately kills older people. He stresses that with age, estrogen and testosterone decline, the "nutrient hormones" that maintain muscle, so you must actively fight this process with protein and strength training; otherwise, muscle loss cannot be reversed.

6:06 Snacking is a modern invention humans never had before
Hyman believes the hunter-gatherer and agricultural eras had no concept of "snacks"; people ate only at meals. The rise of snacking culture directly drove America's obesity and type-2 diabetes epidemics. He barely eats snacks himself, keeping only nuts and jerky as "emergency" food when traveling, to avoid falling into "food emergency mode" and eating carelessly—he admits to a Cinnabon on a delayed flight 20 years ago but hasn't repeated it since.

10:10 Sugar and starch control matters more than any supplement
At 65 with 10% body fat, Hyman sees visceral fat as the real killer; nearly all Americans have it, driving diabetes, obesity, heart disease, cancer, and dementia. He says if this episode could only bring one takeaway, it would be: control sugar and starch—more foundational than any supplement or drug.

11:11 Gluten sensitivity is more common than most people assume
Function's testing runs five different tests for gluten-related antibodies versus the single test most doctors run; antibody levels should be zero normally, and even a slight elevation at 3–4 on the scale means the body is treating gluten as an invader, usually indicating leaky gut. Hyman estimates about 20% of people are gluten-sensitive, noting that modern wheat, after selective breeding, has more gluten protein and amylopectin closer to sugar, often sprayed with glyphosate before harvest.

15:18 GLP-1 drugs cause permanent muscle loss without intervention
Hyman calls the change from GLP-1 "semaglutide face"—rapid loss of facial muscle. He explains that users lose appetite, don't eat enough protein, skip strength training, and the massive muscle lost never comes back, slowing metabolism. After stopping, even at the same weight, they'll eat less and rebound more easily; the key is matching protein intake and strength training during the drug phase.

15:18 Even health-conscious people face severe nutritional deficiencies
Among Function users—already more health-focused than average Americans—70% lack at least one nutrient below "minimum" standards (note: the floor to prevent rickets, not the level truly supporting bone health). This shows the nutritional-density problem in modern diet is worse than it appears.

24:46 Plasmapheresis is a cutting-edge therapy worth trying
Labs funded by Silicon Valley wealth are studying how to clear damaged, aging proteins from the body; plasmapheresis—essentially blood cleaning—is one approach, used in hospitals for decades but now applied to remove inflammatory proteins and toxins. Hyman compares it to Bryan Johnson's "blood swap" experiments with his son and father, calling those "a bit odd," but he'd try plasmapheresis because data supports it and safety is relatively clear.

26:49 Cheap genomics and AI have made prevention affordable
Hyman calls this moment an "Einstein in 1905" one in medical history: first, reframing the body as an interconnected network system, not isolated organs; second, data-acquisition costs collapsing—whole genome sequencing from $1 billion to $300, full-body MRI from $2,500 per knee to $499 total; third, AI as the only tool handling these vast personal biological datasets. The three combined make "accessible preventive medicine" possible for the first time.

item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-11-07-twiv-美国时隔三十年再现麻疹死亡-疫苗怀疑论政策付出代价/

item.description: This week America reported three measles deaths that vaccines could have prevented entirely—New York's first in thirty years, Wisconsin's first in thirty-six. Daniel Griffin attributes them to misinformation from health officials, not public health misfortune.
item.content:encoded:
This week America reported three measles deaths that vaccines could have prevented entirely—New York's first in thirty years, Wisconsin's first in thirty-six. Daniel Griffin attributes them to misinformation from health officials, not public health misfortune.

Information-dense and zero filler: measles deaths, screwworm spread, Ebola's trajectory, and two new studies with surprising findings.

9:20 Measles took three lives in the U.S. this week
Three measles deaths reported this week in America: a child in northern New York (the state's first in thirty years), an unvaccinated adult in Jefferson County, Pennsylvania, and a baby in Wisconsin (the state's first in thirty-six years). Daniel Griffin emphasizes that America had previously eliminated measles—children should not be dying preventably of this vaccine-preventable disease. He directly blames health officials who've undermined the public health system and spread vaccine misinformation, and argues their accountability should rank above political impeachment.

10:25 Autochthonous Chagas disease emerges in a Texas infant
A ten-month-old in Corpus Christi, Texas fell ill with Chagas disease, presenting with high fever, rash, and periorbital swelling. Blood smears confirmed Trypanosoma cruzi, and the infection rapidly progressed to fulminant myocarditis and toxic megacolon. The baby had never left the U.S.; environmental surveys found kissing bugs and animal hosts carrying the parasite in the area, confirming local transmission—likely when the baby ingested the infected insect. The hosts acknowledged that prevention is nearly impossible beyond keeping children indoors, since kissing bugs can penetrate indoor spaces.

17:40 Screwworm cases jump from single digits to over a hundred in months
Screwworm is spreading northward through Texas, New Mexico, and Arizona: four cases in August, three in September, and thirty-six in October brought the total to 113 animal cases by November 5, including a cat in New Mexico. Daniel Griffin showed maps of its progress into central New Mexico, underscoring that this once-eradicated parasitic disease is now advancing north far faster than expected.

18:41 Ebola in DRC shows no sign of slowing
The DRC Ebola outbreak has totaled 10,563 confirmed cases and 5,130 deaths, with no curve inflection—the slope stays constant, a straight upward line. Daniel Griffin points out these numbers have already exceeded the previous largest outbreak (West Africa) in the same timeframe, and most predict it will eventually completely surpass it. The current hope rests on U.S. public health capacity quickly reorganizing to provide assistance.

27:03 Infection in cell culture doesn't mean infection in the human body
A PLOS ONE study infected neural stem cells from human neuroectoderm with pseudoviral particles, finding that Omicron spike protein preferentially entered cells via endocytosis. The authors recommended long-term neurodevelopmental monitoring of infants exposed in utero. But Daniel Griffin cautions that this is petri-dish biology—infected cells in culture don't mean the virus reaches those sites in a living person. Poliovirus replicates in cultured kidney cells but never actually infects human kidneys in real infection.

34:18 Low-dose naltrexone doesn't help long-COVID fatigue
A randomized controlled trial in MedRxiv tested low-dose naltrexone for post-COVID fatigue. Patients accessed a compounding pharmacy, starting at 0.5 mg and titrating to 4.5 mg over 16 weeks of double-blind placebo control. On the primary endpoint of fatigue severity, naltrexone and placebo showed no difference. Given that many long-COVID patients have already tried this drug, this negative result deserves wider awareness.

36:23 Earlier metformin use cuts long-COVID risk more
A target trial emulation study in the Journal of Medical Virology found that starting metformin within six days of COVID diagnosis yielded a 4% incidence of long COVID or death, compared to 8.5% in the control group (treated with fluvoxamine, fluticasone, ivermectin, etc.)—nearly 50% risk reduction. But starting treatment on day 14 showed almost no difference—timing is critical. Daniel Griffin notes the 8.5% long-COVID rate in controls seems high, and the mechanism of response remains unclear, so it's uncertain who should receive the drug.

50:54 COVID vaccines approved for one dose, but protection wanes in six months
Daniel Griffin explains that FDA approval of mRNA COVID vaccines like Comirnaty is for a ‘single dose’, requiring only a minimum two-month interval from any prior dose—not a mandatory six months. In practice, protection declines noticeably around six months but doesn't disappear, so high-risk populations still benefit from another dose then. This year's mRNA flu vaccine could theoretically shift its formulation faster to match circulating strains, but the strain composition this season is identical to traditional egg- and recombinant-based vaccines—no actual advantage taken from the technology.

item.content:encoded:
The $108 billion in convertible notes on the balance sheet is merely accounting revaluation of Google and Amazon's equity stakes as the company's valuation soared—not actual debt.

A financial analyst walks through the most misread numbers in Anthropic's S-1: what convertible notes, net losses, compute efficiency, and hundred-billion-dollar infrastructure spending actually mean.

14:37 Anthropic achieves profitability at IPO, nearly unprecedented in tech history
Anthropic's S-1 shows 85% gross margins, over 20% free cash flow margins, and 8% GAAP operating profit margins. What's striking: Anthropic has raised $141 billion cumulatively (including equity, converts, and SAFEs) yet retains $134 billion in cash, meaning it has burned only $7 billion while generating $16.8 billion in quarterly revenue. Jamin Ball calls this an ‘almost accidentally profitable’ business—software companies almost never achieve positive free cash flow at IPO stage, yet Anthropic has.

17:46 Inference efficiency jumped sevenfold: revenue grew 14 times, compute costs just 2.3 times
Anthropic splits compute between training/internal R&D and model inference for customers; currently only 27% goes to the latter. Comparing year-over-year: inference compute spending grew 2.3x while revenue from inference grew 14x, meaning inference efficiency improved roughly sevenfold. Jamin Ball sees this as evidence of the ‘almost accidentally profitable’ business model—not driven by price increases, but the opposite: they were lowering prices in the same period.

27:09 80% of revenue comes from models launched in the past six months
In the three months ending September, 80% of revenue came from models released less than six months earlier. This exceeds expectations, showing customers have almost entirely migrated to the latest, most capable models rather than staying on older versions. This explains why staying at the frontier is nearly a matter of survival for revenue: once a model falls behind stronger competition, revenue migrates quickly to rivals. Jamin Ball expects this to persist: as open-source models capture share of total tokens consumed, proprietary frontier models capture the dollar share.

37:42 The gap between frontier and open-source models is wider than it appears
To assess the true gap between open-source and frontier models, you cannot compare only published versions, because OpenAI and Anthropic both hold unreleased, stronger models. Jamin Ball cites a chart Mark Chen from OpenAI once showed: on a famous Navier-Stokes math problem, OpenAI's unreleased internal model far surpasses the publicly released Astra. This means the true frontier-open-source gap is much wider than observers see from published products—the opposite of the common narrative that it's narrowing.

46:53 Anthropic's revenue fell when others took the lead, recovered with Opus 5.5
Third-party data shows Anthropic experienced a marked ‘summer decline’: OpenAI's Astra model briefly led, and Kimi K3, GLM series, and DeepSeek collectively gained strength, diverting demand. Revenue from non-Opus 5.5 / Sonnet 5.5 models halved or worse in two to three months. Only the launch of Opus 5.5 and Sonnet 5.5 reignited revenue acceleration. Jamin Ball sees this as proof that staying at the frontier is the direct switch controlling revenue trajectory, not a nice-to-have.

1:12:49 The $108 billion in convertibles on the balance sheet is not actual debt
The roughly $108 billion in convertible notes payable on the balance sheet is not borrowed money but convertible notes that Google and Amazon bought years ago at prices far below today's valuation, revalued each quarter at fair value. They chose converts over direct equity to likely avoid triggering third-party ownership consolidation thresholds under public company accounting rules. As Anthropic's valuation surged, the book value of these liabilities surged with it, but they represent only about $11 billion in actual cash invested, of which roughly $5 billion has already converted to equity, leaving about $6 billion in unconverted principal on the books.

1:14:55 The $80 billion net loss is merely an accounting revaluation side effect
First half results show a net loss of about $8–8.1 billion, but this is not an operating loss. The balance sheet must stay in balance: when convertible notes' fair value surges, liabilities rise, so retained earnings must fall by the same amount. The change in retained earnings flows directly through the income statement as net income or loss. About $7.2 billion of this stems from valuation increases in the convertibles held by Google and Amazon, another roughly $0.9 billion from other notes and SAFEs—all of it is just the accounting reflection of equity appreciation, not actual cash losses. Had they issued equity directly instead of converts, this ‘loss’ would never appear.

1:28:15 Scaling to 30 gigawatts each in five years means $5 trillion in buildout
Jamin Ball estimates on air: if OpenAI and Anthropic each scaled from near zero to 30 gigawatts of capacity in five years, and the two together represent about 40% of total industry capacity, the industry would need about 100 gigawatts of new capacity in five years. At roughly $50 billion per gigawatt of construction cost, five years of buildout would cost about $5 trillion total, or about $1 trillion per year—roughly 5% of US GDP. That scale approaches real-world infrastructure buildout levels, contingent on credit and debt markets being deep and open enough to support it.

She asked tech CEOs their AI acquisition criteria; price never came up unprompted. In this race, securing position beats calculating returns.

Guest experience spans investment banking, private equity, crisis-managing a company as CEO, and media—every claim grounded in specific cases lived through, not theoretical generalizations.

16:22 Your front-line staff will warn you before your executives do
Before the pandemic, Ann Berry's laundry operations team in Las Vegas reported massive order cancellations from Asia. The company—which had already stockpiled PPE and disinfectants from prior avian flu experience—caught the crisis signal first. The lesson: managers must build relationships with front-line workers and not isolate themselves in executive suites, because the earliest warnings typically emerge first in scattered conversations from ground-level staff.

21:34 Operating a company teaches what board questions actually matter
After becoming CEO of a hotel laundry company during the pandemic, Ann Berry called CEOs from her past PE roles to apologize. She admitted the 'value-add suggestions' she'd pitched in boardrooms based on spreadsheet data had been annoying. Once she owned operations and held the P&L, she understood what boards should actually scrutinize and which due diligence questions had real weight.

37:52 Walmart became a tech stock by monetizing advertising data
In 2022, Ann Berry wrote that Walmart's e-commerce data was spawning an advertising business now worth nearly $65 billion annually. The company moved its listing to Nasdaq to reinforce the tech-company narrative. She views this as a legacy retailer's successful reinvention through data assets—not a dinosaur awaiting Amazon's extinction event.

43:56 State legislatures will likely ban dynamic pricing
She predicts California, New York, and similar states will lead in banning dynamic pricing—when retailers use license plates, shopping cart sensors, or credit scores to set different prices. Walmart once tested raising mayo prices when tuna was detected in a cart. Consumer backlash will accelerate legislation, especially as inflation already strains trust. Otherwise, an 'AI surcharge' layer compounds the damage.

45:58 Brands and retailers must now court AI shopping agents
At a Mexico City retail summit, Liverpool department store's CEO raised a novel question: as AI agents shop on behalf of consumers, brands and retailers must research how to win agent preference and visibility—mirroring how they've studied consumer marketing. Ann Berry considers this inevitable: it will reshape how retailers control data and manage product exposure.

49:00 AI capex isn't a bubble—it's that returns are unmeasurable
She rejects ‘this is the dot-com bubble all over again’ analogies. Today's funded AI companies have real revenue and profit, unlike Pets.com with just a concept. The genuine problem: scan earnings calls and analyst reports, and almost nobody explains what actual ROI these capital outlays will generate or when. Early-stage investing has also sobered considerably since the 2021 NFT and Web3 manias.

56:07 Tech giants acquire emerging threats before they can scale
Fei-Fei Li's World Models acquisition by AMD exemplifies Ann Berry's concept ‘flight to scale’: the billions raised by OpenAI, Anthropic and peers are deployed to acquire every early-stage company that could become competitive. She frames this not as safety-driven but as fundamentally about market dominance—well-capitalized incumbents preempting threats rather than purely defending turf.

57:10 When tech giants acquire companies, price gets mentioned last
In interviews with major tech company CEOs and CFOs on acquisition criteria, answers focus on technology fit, product adjacency, team, and culture—price surfaces only when Ann Berry specifically asks. She recalls Marc Andreessen once saying that investing works on home runs, so overpaying by 2x for Facebook wouldn't matter. Big tech now applies that same logic to AI acquisitions.

item.content:encoded:
Brian notes that the government never defined what ‘strategic national interests’ are, so it cannot convince Congress to keep funding it—consequently, both the defense authorization and appropriations bills are stuck in continuing resolutions until the war somehow ends.

From the Iran stalemate, congressional budget freeze, to Pentagon infighting, this episode explains the cascade of consequences after the midterm elections all at once—essential for those watching defense policy.

1:02 No victory theory, Congress won't fund it
Brian Clark notes that the government never defined what ‘strategic national interests’ in Iran are, so even if polling is unfavorable, it cannot convince Congress to keep funding. After the midterm elections, the White House urgently needs an off-ramp it can package as a ‘victory,’ but Iran has no incentive to cooperate; meanwhile, Congress is unwilling to pass the NDAA and appropriations bills, forcing the budget to rely on continuing resolutions until the war somehow ends.

12:29 Naval withdrawal from Middle East teaches the PLA an unexpected lesson
As Iran's blockade requires the US Navy to maintain freedom of navigation, CENTCOM has consumed about half of the active deployed fleet; once this force withdraws, Iran can immediately re-seal the Strait of Hormuz. At the same time, the Coast Guard has relocated all 6 rapid response patrol boats originally stationed in the Persian Gulf to Singapore, where they operate with South China Sea assets—good for PACOM but for CENTCOM it means a contraction in America's naval presence in the Middle East, which the PLA could read as a successful model of ‘making America abandon near-shore bases.’

20:47 The president watches oil prices, not Iran's intentions
The show notes that intelligence systems can provide ‘valuable’ information about Iran's leadership intentions, economic conditions, domestic unrest monitoring, and so on, but what actually determines the White House's judgment is numbers like gas prices. A president elected on oil prices and economic issues will naturally evaluate this war's prospects through a narrower, more optimistic lens than one based on more comprehensive battlefield intelligence.

21:51 Americans never truly cared whether Iran has nuclear weapons
The episode makes a ‘revealed preference’ argument: this war let Americans for the first time truly feel the pain of rising gas prices, unlike the War on Terror where only some communities bore the costs; public reaction shows that while everyone says Iran cannot have nuclear weapons, when facing real economic pain, people ask whether it's worth it. Compared with North Korea and Pakistan, whose nuclear weapons brought no ‘provable change,’ the narrative that ‘Iran must never have nuclear weapons’ becomes harder to defend.

34:24 Larger Democratic majorities paradoxically stabilize the defense budget
The discussion suggests that if Democrats won a larger majority rather than a narrow one, the 20-30 bipartisan members in Congress who demand ‘10% budget cuts’ every year would lose their swing-vote power, actually giving leadership more room to keep the budget nominally flat (which still means real cuts after inflation, but not dramatic ones). At the same time, procurement officials previously, to avoid offending ‘the boss of the boss,’ habitually kept politically connected companies on candidate lists; this incentive would tighten as Democrats strengthen oversight.

37:31 Starshield will eventually be forced to separate
The show cites a concrete precedent: the Pentagon's prior concerns about Claude/Anthropic were validated—on non-classified systems, the company could remotely downgrade models without notifying customers (it happened with Fable's release), confirming the military's concern that ‘you cannot give this much control to a single commercial company.’ The same logic will eventually apply to Starshield: once it becomes the backbone for military communications and command-and-control, and Musk holds actual operational control despite lacking security clearance, this arrangement won't be tolerated long.

42:58 Defense-tech VCs may pull out of early-stage rounds
As PE/VC funds that flooded into defense tech after the Russia-Ukraine war start seeking returns, there's concern they'll retreat from seed and Series A rounds, leaving only well-funded ‘neoprimes’ sustaining valuations through acquisitions of smaller companies (like Shield AI's recent deals), effectively rebuilding a new traditional military-industrial complex. The show believes this will slow innovation—compare DIU's drone competitions held only every six months with Ukraine's capability iteration cycle of just six to twelve hours.

1:03:51 In Team Yankee, the body count is deliberately left blank
The book discussion covers a scene in Team Yankee: the protagonist watches burning Soviet tanks and infantry fighting vehicles, mentally calculates that each carries 12 people, but doesn't finish the thought—the author deliberately doesn't calculate for the reader ‘I just killed 36 people,’ forcing readers to complete the thought themselves. The discussion also notes that officers must learn to shut up and execute ‘lawful but disapproved’ orders, echoing the narrator's own near-isolation in southern Syria.

item.title: Saturated fat wrongly blamed: real health risk hides in food processing
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-11-06-foundmyfitness-饱和脂肪被冤枉-真正的健康风险藏在食物被加工的方式里/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-11-06-foundmyfitness-饱和脂肪被冤枉-真正的健康风险藏在食物被加工的方式里/
item.description: Same saturated fat, opposite effects: butter raises LDL, raw cream doesn't—health risk comes from food processing, not fat type itself.
item.content:encoded:
Same saturated fat, opposite effects: butter raises LDL, raw cream doesn't—health risk comes from food processing, not fat type itself.

Three hours of high-density information: controlled butter-versus-cream experiments, tobacco companies' acquisition of food giants, and cutting-edge obesity science—nearly every segment challenges decades-old diet advice.

9:11 The same saturated fat, butter and cream have vastly different effects
The milk fat globule membrane exists in milk, cheese, and yogurt, but butter production destroys and discards it. This membrane contains sphingolipids and phospholipids that interact with intestinal microbes and reduce cholesterol absorption. One 8-week randomized European trial directly compared butter and raw cream with identical saturated fat content: the butter group's LDL increased, the raw cream group's LDL didn't budge. This demolishes the claim that all saturated fat is equally harmful. What matters is food's complete structure, not the fat molecules alone.

29:17 Heart disease adopted the single-nutrient logic of vitamin-deficiency diseases
In the 1930s, scientists defeated vitamin-deficiency diseases by targeting single nutrients—niacin and vitamin C. When heart disease became America's leading cause of death in the 1950s-80s, scientists almost instinctively asked the same question: "Which nutrient causes this?" The answer: saturated fat. But heart disease, obesity, and diabetes aren't single-nutrient deficiencies. This historical accident directly shaped three decades of low-fat diet guidelines.

46:28 Red meat's real threat is heme iron, not saturated fat
Red meat damages through heme iron and specific inflammatory compounds, not saturated fat. Excess heme iron drives inflammation and oxidative stress, directly harming pancreatic beta cells—which explains why red meat's link to type 2 diabetes is stronger than to heart disease. Cooking method matters: charring and grilling generate carcinogens like heterocyclic amines. Side dishes matter too—cruciferous vegetables contain compounds that detoxify these carcinogens and flip red meat's net health effect. Same meat, different preparation: opposite outcomes.

59:38 Omega-6 unfairly blamed: three plausible-sounding but wrong reasons
Consumer belief that seed oils are harmful stems from three ‘partial truths’: industrial trans fats from the 1950s onward were wrongly equated with seed oils; ultra-processed foods' processing methods and contaminants raised alarm but were blamed on the oil; Omega-6 versus Omega-3 competition theory from rodent studies got mistakenly applied to humans. Yet dozens of randomized human trials prove Omega-6 doesn't cause inflammation. It actually reduces insulin resistance, lowers A1C, reduces LDL and triglycerides, and raises HDL.

1:20:51 Tobacco companies transplanted addiction science into the food industry
From the late 1970s to the 1980s, the two largest U.S. tobacco companies—R.J. Reynolds and Philip Morris—acquired nearly every major food brand. They then transferred their addiction scientists, flavor scientists, and child-marketing teams directly into food operations. This fundamentally differs from low-fat guidelines, which were sincere but mistaken. Here the goal was pure addictiveness, not nutrition. Tobacco litigation unearthed internal memos proving it. This was food industry's true turning point.

1:29:57 Food stripped of cellular structure deals a triple blow to the body
Ultra-processed foods destroy the natural cellular matrix, causing threefold harm: First, nutrient absorption speeds up—Cheerios remain labeled whole-grain but become functionally like white bread after reprocessing, spiking blood sugar nearly identically. Second, gut microbes starve—20% of food calories normally feed the colon microbiota and generate beneficial metabolites, but ultra-processed foods divert those calories elsewhere. Third, calorie distribution inverts—eating whole foods, your body absorbs 75-80% while microbes get 20-25%, but ultra-processed foods flip this: you might absorb 99%. This calorie-allocation concept is recent, underexplored, and widely ignored.

1:50:09 Obesity's real cause isn't eating more; it's the body burning less
Before 2000, the logic was straightforward: more calories plus less movement equals obesity. Post-2000 revealed a paradox. Doubly labeled water—objective measurement—shows calorie intake flat or dropping; actual physical activity rose with gym memberships, marathons, and yoga classes all increasing; yet obesity accelerated anyway. Recent science points to the culprit: average resting energy expenditure in the U.S. and U.K. fell 220 calories daily, enough to explain the entire obesity epidemic. Scientists have barely investigated this phenomenon.

2:13:22 New dietary guidelines explicitly name ultra-processed foods and additives for the first time
Compared with the past two or three decades, these new guidelines represent a major change: they explicitly require real food and ban ultra-processed and packaged products, specifically prohibiting sugar-sweetened beverages, candy, artificial sweeteners, artificial colors, and artificial preservatives—restrictions affecting roughly 50-60% of U.S. food supply. Previously, USDA had to balance guidelines against food industry interests, so avoided direct condemnation of processed foods; it just preached ‘any food works if you meet the nutrition benchmarks.’ That compromise is gone.

item.content:encoded:
Investment banks lock people in with non-competes and vesting; law-firm partners are protected by legal ethics and cannot be locked down—this is why Weil Gotshal collapsed overnight and investment banks do not.

The first half is low-density election-night chat; the middle on law-firm partner runs and the ending on the Binance hack are where the content is—worth a separate listen.

5:06 Prediction markets sell certainty, not accuracy
Matt watched Kalshi on election night as Democratic Senate control climbed from about 73% to about 98%; once it hit 98%, he went to sleep. He admits knowing the result three or four hours early has zero economic value for ordinary people, but says the real value is compressing noisy speculation and contradictory signals on Twitter into a single number—so you don't have to stay up waiting for the vote count. That's underrated social utility, not a trading tool.

9:11 80% is not 98%; never conflate the two
Two discuss probability calibration: if an event is tagged at 80% probability, one in five times it won't happen—Brazil's election saw Bolsonaro flip from around 80%. On US Senate election night, odds climbed to 98% before Matt felt safe sleeping. He stresses that well-calibrated probabilities and near-certainty are different things; at 80% on voting day, ‘anything could happen’.

16:15 Election results tanked data-center stocks
The midterms became a proxy for data-center expansion—many candidates from both parties called for pausing construction; the market read Democratic gains as bad news. CoreWeave fell about 10% that day, SpaceX-related plays weakened too. A rare instance of election results actually moving real-asset prices.

18:19 Manufacturing progress for AI chips depends on irreplaceable human craft
Matt read a New Yorker piece on chip supply chains and thought: you sneeze in a TSMC factory, you set back AI progress three years. Ultraprecise manufacturing ultimately depends on an old master who taps the equipment by feel—perhaps five people globally know how. Anthropic says Claude can design next-generation chips and fabs, but Claude cannot train this master's hand feel. This reveals overlooked physical fragility in the AI narrative.

24:40 Law firms cannot hold onto their moneymaking partners
Weil Gotshal's collapse traces to a partner run. Citing Yale Law professor John Morley's research, collapsing firms are often not in bad financial shape; the problem is top earners get poached by more lucrative private-equity platforms. When they leave, average partner profit drops, so the rest also leave, and the firm hollows out. Investment banks can lock people in with non-competes, garden leave, and vesting schedules; law firms cannot.

26:40 Legal ethics block the tools that let investment banks hold partners
Matt explains the key difference: professional legal ethics bars lawyers from being restricted from practicing, so law firms cannot lock partners down with equity vesting like investment banks can—only clawback equity over reasonable periods when they leave. These rules were designed for a traditional gentleman-partnership era and completely fail in today's highly commercialized, high-turnover market. Law firms must compete in a far freer market than investment banks, without investment banks' lockup tools.

35:53 Reversible transactions are not a stablecoin flaw; they are a feature
North Korean hackers used social engineering posing as job interviews to steal $6.3 billion in crypto from Binance; roughly half was in centralized stablecoins like Tether and USDC. Because stablecoins are essentially ledger entries in the issuer's system, Tether and Circle simply reversed the stolen transfers. The other half—real on-chain crypto—could not be reversed. Matt sees centralized stablecoins' reversible transactions not as a betrayal of crypto principles but as superior design.

39:54 Forty minutes between theft and freeze is the launderer's whole window
From Binance theft to Tether and Circle freeze took about 40 minutes—bridged by direct calls among finance executives, not blockchain. In that window, hackers went wild buying Ethereum on DEXes, pushing the price up 15%, and took bad execution. But a 15% slippage is still cheap for money laundering. More ironic: the market-makers who filled those orders later told Bloomberg they made a killing on the trades.
